title: Introducing The Practice Project
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: The author announces The Practice Project, a joint AEI and researchED initiative producing practitioner-focused papers translating cognitive science and education research into classroom guidance. The project's thesis is that the next phase of education reform must move beyond systemic change to focus on improving what teachers actually do in classrooms. The first two papers challenge prominent misconceptions: one argues that explicit instruction outperforms student-centered approaches despite what education schools teach, and another argues that critical thinking cannot be separated from domain knowledge and taught as a transferable skill. Upcoming papers will cover mathematics, assessment, history, student work analysis, science, and reading. The goal is to produce durable reference resources that teachers annotate and return to, filling a gap where education has opinions in abundance but accessible professional knowledge in short supply.
points: The Practice Project (AEI and researchED) translates cognitive science into practical classroom guidance for teachers, coaches, and school leaders.
Policy creates conditions for success; student learning ultimately depends on what teachers know and can do.
The first paper argues explicit instruction outperforms student-centered approaches despite prevailing teacher education assumptions.
The second paper argues critical thinking cannot be taught as a transferable skill — it depends on domain knowledge.
The goal is durable reference resources teachers return to, not articles read once and forgotten.
quotes: Policy can only create the conditions for success. Ultimately, student learning depends on what teachers know and are able to do.
Rather than prescribing new policies, adjudicating arguments, or promoting educational fashions, the papers in this initiative focus on the craft of teaching itself.
Explicit Instruction Works. Education Schools Just Won't Admit It.
Critical thinking depends on knowledge rather than existing apart from it.
Education has no shortage of opinions. What it often lacks is an accessible body of professional knowledge that practitioners can rely on to hone their craft.
